name: Philosophy as preparation for death (moderate asceticism)
plain_explanation: The true philosopher does not fear death but welcomes it, since it frees the soul from the body's distractions; but Plato's ideal philosopher is not a harsh ascetic who struggles against pleasure -- he simply becomes absorbed in higher things and forgets bodily indulgence.
precise_definition: Plato's portrait of the philosophic life as one in which bodily pleasures (food, drink, sex, adornment) are not forbidden by effortful self-denial but are naturally neglected because the philosopher's attention is fixed on the soul and the pursuit of truth, so that the resulting asceticism is 'not, properly speaking, ascetic' in intention.
why_it_mattered: Russell uses it to make an important ethical point: bodily pleasure is not the only kind of pleasure, and some of the worst human vices (love of power, cruelty, envy) are purely mental, so indifference to bodily pleasure does not by itself guarantee virtue.
examples: Socrates, though indifferent to wine, could out-drink anyone without becoming intoxicated -- it was not drinking he condemned, but pleasure in drinking.
Russell's own observation: 'I have known many philosophers who forgot their meals, and read a book when at last they did eat.'
objections: Russell: this view, popularized, becomes genuinely ascetic and can mislead moralists into thinking anyone who avoids bodily pleasure must be virtuous -- but 'the worst pleasures, as well as the best, are mental,' citing envy, cruelty, and love of power (with Hitler given as a contemporary example).
influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell connects the mistaken popularized version to real historical harm done by ecclesiastics who, having renounced bodily pleasure, became dominated by unchecked love of power.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Echoes Orphic notions of ritual 'purity,' reinterpreted by Plato as freedom from bodily slavery.
